moves.spoken: Another King's Indian — having just spent so long talking about it, we might as well play it.
White grabs the centre with c4, and Black fianchettoes with g6 — the King's Indian in motion.
The bishop settles on g7, staring down the long diagonal at White's centre.
White builds the big pawn centre with e4, and Black holds back with d6 — the classic King's Indian restraint, meaning to strike at that centre later.
Development and castling, both kings tucked safely away.
White plays the main line with the bishop to e2, and Black challenges the centre with e5.
White castles into the main line.
Now a line Black likes — the capture on d4, and in effect Black has reached a Maroczy-type structure by transposition.
White takes back with the knight.
The rook lifts to e8, and here is the subtle difference: Black's c-pawn is still home rather than committed to e7, which gives the rook a clear line of fire down the file at the e4-pawn.
White props up the centre with f3. So how does Black build on that pressure against e4 — what breakthrough can be prepared?
And there it is, c6 — the main, combative line, staking a share of the centre. The knight to c6 was also possible, but c6 is the fighting choice.
White tucks the king to h1 — a strong prophylactic move, stepping off the exposed diagonal and out of future tactics. He knows the theory.
And Black's thematic reply, the knight out to h5 — no surprise to anyone who has watched a King's Indian: it frees the f-pawn and opens ideas like the queen to h4.

White develops the bishop to e3 — but notice, it has landed on a square where it is momentarily undefended, and Black's rook on e8 is already x-raying down the file. How to bring those two facts together?
The answer is f5 — the pawn heading for f4, aiming to plant a knight on g3 as a permanent thorn, and combining with the rook's pressure down the e-file.
White covers f4 with the queen to d2, and Black asks the Shankland question — what if we push f4 anyway?
And Black does exactly that — f4 regardless. If White grabs it, Black recaptures and drops the knight into f4 with a monster outpost.
White sidesteps with the bishop to f2.
Now the typical regrouping — the bishop centralises on e5, a gorgeous outpost, and a very thematic sacrifice is coming into view.
White retreats the knight to c2 — but the sacrifice can be unleashed at once.
There it is — not the d5 break, which White has clamped down, but the knight to g3 with check, a hallmark King's Indian idea.

White steps the king back to g1. Now you would think Black simply grabs the rook on f1 — but here is the mind-bender: against another grandmaster, yes, take the exchange; this time Black is playing for checkmate.
The queen swings to h4, joining the hunt — mate is the goal now.
White finds a really strong defensive move, the bishop to d4, drawing the sting from the attack.
That bishop to d4 was excellent, so Black cashes in and takes the exchange on f1 rather than let the chance slip.
White recaptures. Black is up the exchange — and now the golden rule: the single biggest cause of disaster after winning material is to stop playing good moves. So Black keeps developing.
The bishop comes to e6, continuing development — no coasting.
White helps out by trading on e5, which only cements Black's pawns and structure.
To consolidate the extra exchange, Black just needs to finish developing — the knight out, a rook to d8 — while keeping the pawn safe. Can Black do both at once?
The knight to d7 is the move, and Black can always prise the queen off its perch with the queen to e7 next.
Up the exchange, White goes hunting pawns with the queen to c7.
A good try, but Black offers the queen trade with the queen to d8, simplifying toward the win.
White takes the queen.
Black recaptures toward d8 — and against the alternative queen retreat, the trade was prepared anyway.
White centralises the king. Now, for the attentive — where does Black's knight belong?
The knight to c5 — the same King's Indian idea survives into the ending: Black eyes a check on d2 that would win the knight.
To cement the knight, Black brings the other rook to d8, and a5 is always available to keep White from chasing it away.
And Black plays a5 to do exactly that — even in an endgame, the typical middlegame ideas still apply.
Now the king joins in.
And Black opens the kingside with g5 — playing it exactly as if it were a middlegame, because the same ideas apply.
Black keeps rolling on the kingside with h5.
The king steps up to f6, right into the game.
A textbook King's Indian picture — and with the c6-pawn guarding d5, Black is free to push on the kingside.
So Black pushes the pawn to g4 — it breaks the position open and even clears a path for the king to march to g3, the Russian-school way.
The h-file opens, and a highway appears for the king.
White scrambles the knight back to f2 to defend.
Instead of walking the king in, Black clamps with g3. Doesn't that lock the position in White's favour? No — watch the g2-pawn.
The obvious jump does not work; Black looks for a more methodical way to pile on the g2-pawn.
So a rook that has done its job reroutes — flexibility of thinking. Don't stay attached to a piece's square once its work is done.
The rook swings to h2, deep into White's position.
And always look for the loose piece — White's knight on c2 is undefended, and the x-rays are lining up.
There it is — the bishop to h3, a textbook idea, forcing the g2-pawn forward; then Black wins the knight and promotes, or forces White to give up the bishop for the pawn. The game is over.
White wriggles the knight to e2, but it is far too late.
Black simply takes on g2.
The knight to g1 attacks nothing.
So Black just scoops the bishop.
And Black grabs the knight off c2 with the rook. Now the passed pawn marches home, or a check and promotion — and White resigns.

Looking back, the king to h1 was a sound prophylactic move. The critical theoretical test is g4, sending the knight back to f6 — it weakens White's kingside, but there is a wild knight sacrifice on d5, worked out a few years ago, that has cast real doubt on this whole line at the top. And yet — not being fully sound at grandmaster level is no reason at all not to play it.
